blocks.x: Sometimes, making it to the gym is a big ask. Maybe you want to catch up on sleep, your social calendar is stacked, or you’re working late hours before your next performance review. But there’s one workout that makes the classic “I don’t have time” excuse harder to defend—and that’s because it only takes seven minutes.

The 7-minute workout isn’t the latest fad on TikTok. It’s been around for over a decade, and promises a legitimate sweat in less time than you’ll spend waiting in line at Whole Foods. It sounds suspiciously convenient—but how much can seven minutes of exercise realistically accomplish?
What is the 7-minute workout?

Developed by exercise physiologist Chris Jordan, the 7-minute workout is a high-intensity circuit training (HICT) protocol designed to cram cardio and bodyweight resistance work into a tiny window. When it debuted in 2013, it gained popularity for how brief—and apparently effective—it is.
Despite the oddly specific number, there’s nothing physiologically magical about seven minutes. What matters more is how much quality work you complete in that time frame.

The original 7-minute workout calls for 12 exercises, performing them for 30 seconds each with 10 seconds of rest in between. Raymond Agostino, DPT, a physical therapist, sports performance coach, and owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida, says 30 seconds is long enough to accumulate meaningful work but short enough to keep the intensity relatively high. And don’t expect much salvation from those 10-second breaks. They’re really transition periods, not full recovery, and your heart rate stays elevated as you move onto the next exercise. The order of the moves matters, too: They’re deliberately sequenced so you’re not torching the same muscles back-to-back.

The formula has spawned plenty of variations, but the OG protocol in the original paper, published in 2013 in the American College of Sports Medicine’s Health & Fitness Journal, calls for the following sequence:
Jumping jacks
Wall sit
Push-up
Abdominal crunch
Step-up onto a chair
Squat
Tricep dip on a chair
Plank
High knees/running in place
Lunge
Push-up and rotation

Benefits of the 7-minute workout
The 7-minute workout is much shorter than your average gym session. Still, if you’re actually working hard, it’s enough to provide meaningful benefits.

According to Alex Rothstein, EdD, MS, CSCS, an exercise physiologist and coordinator of the exercise Science program at New York Institute of Technology, the biggest payoff is for conditioning: think cardiorespiratory fitness, metabolic adaptations, and muscular endurance. You may get some strength and muscle-building stimulus, too—particularly if you’re less trained—but that's more of a modest bonus than the main attraction. There’s also good potential for calorie- and fat-burning, he adds.

Efficiency and accessibility are natural draws for this method. “You can challenge your cardiovascular system and muscular endurance simultaneously without needing a gym, complicated equipment, or a large block of your day,” says Agostino. It’s attractive for frequent travelers, people squeezed for time, or anyone who has trouble talking themselves into a longer workout. If you’re in the latter group, the 7-minute workout can be compelling since it’s basically over by the time your brain comes up with an excuse to opt out of it.
For a few minutes and no barbells or bikes in sight, it’s a pretty decent bargain—especially when the alternative is sitting on the couch.
Where it falls short

The same thing that makes the 7-minute workout so appealing is also its clearest weak point: Seven minutes doesn’t offer much training volume. “That becomes particularly important if your goals are maximizing strength, muscle growth, power, or endurance,” says Agostino. Plus, bodyweight exercises have their limitations. Eventually, your muscles get wise to the same squats, push-ups, and lunges. You'll need some form of progressive overload—more resistance, more volume, or other ways to up the challenge—to continue making gains.

The authors of the original paper even call out the workout’s shortcomings. “Although HICT can be an efficient means by which to improve health and decrease body fat, it may be inferior to creating absolute strength and power, specific endurance, and other specific performance variables,” they write.

There’s also a basic programming problem: the OG circuit isn’t fully balanced. You’ll push, squat, lunge, and plank your way through it, but there’s virtually no pulling work for your back, Agostino points out.

It could also be tricky for beginners. Rothstein wouldn’t suggest newbies head straight into seven minutes of near-maximal work. “Their bodies might not be able to tolerate such high intensities—exercise like this can be very strenuous and unpleasant—and they’re at risk of bad form and injury,” he says. On the other hand, Agostino casts a wider net and says beginners could ease into things by modifying exercises, slowing down, or taking longer rest periods.

Even for fitness buffs, racing the clock comes with its own downsides. Both experts warn that form can start to unravel when fatigue hits, and it can be easy to sacrifice movement quality while maintaining intensity.

And then there’s a significant asterisk attached to the whole 7-minute premise. The original paper actually recommends repeating the circuit two to three times. Do that, and your conveniently bite-sized workout suddenly becomes a full meal. But this recommendation doesn’t mean that a single set is worthless; additional rounds offer more training volume that the 7-minute version inherently lacks.
So do 7-minute workouts work?

Yes, the 7-minute workout actually works. “It’s not a gimmick and any exercise is better than no exercise—particularly if it is at a high enough intensity to promote physiological change,” Rothstein says. Still, it won’t cover all your bases. The biggest takeaway: If your primary goals are maximal strength or muscle size, this protocol shouldn’t be first on your list.

So who’s the best fit to give the 7-minute workout a go? The sweet spot is for someone who’s already comfortable with exercising but is crunched for time—like the guy who’s at the office from dawn til dusk or anyone who knows that an hourlong workout simply isn’t in the cards that day. Agostino calls it a minimum viable workout, which may be the best way to think about it.

If you’re keen to try it, just have it complement your existing cardio and resistance training routine—not replace it. “Seven minutes is enough to matter, but that doesn’t necessarily mean seven minutes is enough for everything,” says Agostino.
